78.4. For while almost all the others who had shared in the lawlessness against the oracle had met with the fitting punishment from the divine power, as we recorded a little before, he alone, having escaped the notice of the divine, undertook to incite the mercenaries to revolt.

78.5. For he said that Timoleon, being out of his mind, was leading the soldiers to acknowledged destruction; for the Carthaginians being sixfold in number and insurpassable in all their preparations, he promised to defeat them, gambling away the lives of the mercenaries, and not even having paid the pay owed for a long time because of his poverty.
78.6. He advised, then, to turn back to Syracuse and demand the pay, and not to follow on a hopeless campaign.

79.1. The mercenaries gladly receiving his words and trying to make a mutiny, Timoleon, scarcely, after many entreaties and promising gifts, stopped the disturbance. Nevertheless, a thousand having followed Thrasius, he postponed their punishment to another time, and writing to his friends in Syracuse to receive them graciously and pay them, he wholly quenched all the disturbance, but took away from those who disobeyed the glory that came from the victory.

79.2. He himself, restoring the rest by humane intercourse to their former goodwill, advanced against the enemy, who were encamped not far off. Gathering the soldiers into an assembly and through his words instilling courage into the multitude, he went through the unmanliness of the Phoenicians and reminded them of the success of Gelon.

79.3. All shouting, as if with one voice, to attack the barbarians and begin the battle, mules happening to be bringing parsley for the bedding, Timoleon said that he accepted the omen of victory; for the Isthmian crown is made of parsley.

79.4. The soldiers, at Timoleon's order, plaiting crowns of the parsley and putting them about their heads, advanced with joy, as if the gods were signifying victory to them beforehand; which also came to pass.

79.5. For they got the better of the enemy, beyond hope, not only through their own valour, but also through the cooperation of the gods. For Timoleon, drawing up his force, came down from certain hills to the river Crimisus, and ten thousand having already crossed, he dashed against these at the first onset, himself stationed in the middle of the phalanx.

79.6. A fierce battle taking place, and the Greeks being superior both in valour and in skill of hand, there was great slaughter of the barbarians. As those who had crossed were now fleeing, the whole force of the Carthaginians, crossing the stream, set right the defeat of their own men.

80.1. The battle being renewed, and the Phoenicians by their numbers encompassing the Greeks, suddenly a great storm of rain broke from the surrounding sky, and a quantity of large hail, and lightnings and thunders with great winds swooped down; and all these things being driven by the storm against the backs of the Greeks but the faces of the barbarians, Timoleon's men easily endured the occurrence, while the Phoenicians, unable to bear the magnitude of the circumstance, and at the same time the Greeks pressing upon them, took to flight.

80.2. As all turned toward the river, cavalry and foot mingled together, and the chariots confounded along with these, some, trampled by one another and pierced by the swords and spears of their own allies, had a calamity past help; while others, driven in droves by the enemy cavalry into the river's stream and receiving their wounds in the back, died.

80.3. And many were destroyed without an enemy's blow, the bodies being heaped up through fear and the multitude and the difficulties in the stream. But the greatest thing was that, the rains having become violent, the river, borne down with a more forcible current, submerged many and destroyed them as they swam across with their arms.

80.4. At last, of the Carthaginians, those who filled the Sacred Band, being in number two thousand five hundred, and being foremost all of them in valour and reputation, and moreover in property, fighting brilliantly, were cut down.

80.5. Of the others who campaigned with them, there died more than ten thousand, and there were taken captive no fewer than fifteen thousand. Of the chariots, most were shattered in the struggle, and two hundred were taken; and the baggage-carriers and the teams and the multitude of the waggons fell into the hands of the Greeks.

80.6. Of the arms, most were destroyed by the river, but to Timoleon's tent a thousand breastplates and more than ten thousand shields were carried off. Of these, some were later dedicated in the temples in Syracuse, some divided among the allies, and some Timoleon sent to Corinth, ordering that they be dedicated in the temple of Poseidon.

81.1. Much money too having been taken, because the Carthaginians had a quantity of silver and gold drinking-cups and, moreover, surpassing other adornment because of the magnitude of their wealth, he granted to the soldiers to keep all of it as prizes of their valour.

81.2. Of the Carthaginians, those who escaped the danger in the battle scarcely got safe to Lilybaeum. So great a dismay and fear held them that they did not dare to embark on the ships nor sail off to Libya, supposing that, through the gods' enmity toward them, they would be swallowed up by the Libyan sea.

81.3. Those in Carthage, learning of the magnitude of the calamity, were crushed in their spirits and supposed that Timoleon would speedily come against them with his force. Straightway they brought back Gescon the son of Hanno, who had been banished, and appointed him general, because he seemed to excel in audacity and generalship.

81.4. And they themselves resolved not to risk citizen persons, but to gather foreign mercenaries and especially Greeks; and they supposed that many would respond to them for the campaign because of the magnitude of the pay and the wealth of Carthage. To Sicily they sent suitable envoys, ordering them to make peace on whatever terms might be possible.

82.1. This year having passed, Lysimachides was archon at Athens, and in Rome consuls had been appointed, Quintus Servilius and Marcus Rutilius. In their time Timoleon, returning to Syracuse, first drove out of the city all the mercenaries who had abandoned him, those with Thrasius, as being traitors.

82.2. These, crossing into Italy and seizing a certain place by the sea in Bruttium, plundered it. The Bruttii, provoked, straightway marched against them with a great force, and taking the place by siege, shot them all down. The mercenaries, then, who abandoned Timoleon, met with such a calamity as the reward of their own lawlessness.

82.3. Timoleon, having arrested Postumius the Tyrrhenian, who plundered those sailing with twelve pirate vessels and had sailed in to Syracuse as a friend, put him to death. He received also graciously the settlers sent out by the Corinthians, being five thousand in number. After this the Carthaginians, sending envoys and entreating much, he granted them peace, on terms that all the Greek cities should be free, and that the river called Lycus should be the boundary of the dominions of both; and that the Carthaginians should not be permitted to help the tyrants who warred against the Syracusans.

82.4. After this, having subdued Hicetas, he put him to death, and besieging the Campanians in Aetna, destroyed them. And Nicodemus the tyrant of the Centoripini, having struck him with terror, he drove out of the city, and Apolloniades the ruler of the Agyrinaeans, putting an end to his tyranny, made the freed men Syracusans. In general, having rooted out all the tyrants in the island and freed the cities, he received them into the alliance.

82.5. When he had proclaimed throughout Greece that the Syracusans were giving land and houses to those who wished to share in the citizenship in Syracuse, many Greeks came to the allotment; and at last settlers were appointed, to the undivided Syracusan territory forty thousand, and to the territory of Agyrium ten thousand, because of the magnitude and beauty of the country.

82.6. Straightway too he corrected the existing laws in Syracuse, which Diocles had drawn up. And those concerning private contracts or inheritances he left unchanged, but those legislated concerning public matters he corrected, with a view to his own purpose, as seemed at the time to be advantageous.

82.7. The overseer and corrector of the legislation was Cephalus the Corinthian, a man esteemed for education and intelligence. After these things he resettled the Leontines in Syracuse, and, adding settlers to the Camarinaean territory, enlarged the city.

83.1. In general, having peacefully settled all the affairs in Sicily, he made the cities quickly take on great increase toward prosperity. For from long ago, because of the strife and the civil wars, and moreover the multitude of tyrants ever rising up, the cities were desolate of inhabitants, and the lands, through neglect, had become wild and barren of cultivated crops; but then, because of the multitude of settlers that flowed in, and because of the long-continued peace that had supervened, they were tamed by cultivation and brought forth many crops of every kind. These the Sicilian Greeks, selling profitably to the merchants, quickly rose again in their fortunes.

83.2. Accordingly, because of the abundance from these things, many great offerings were constructed in those times; in Syracuse the building near the Meson, called of the sixty couches, which surpassed in size and construction the works in Sicily, which Agathocles the ruler constructed, but which, because of the weight of the works overtopping the temples of the gods, met with a sign of displeasure from the divine power, being struck by lightning; and the towers by the small harbour, having their inscriptions of stones of different kinds, signifying the name of the one who constructed them, Agathocles; and likewise to these, a little later, by Hieron the king, both the Olympieium in the market-place and the altar near the theatre, a furlong in length, and having its height and breadth in proportion to this.

83.3. And in the smaller cities, among which the city of the Agyrinaeans is counted, which shared in the allotment of that time because of the aforesaid abundance from the crops, it constructed a theatre, the most beautiful in Sicily after that of the Syracusans, and temples of the gods and a council-house and a market-place, and moreover considerable constructions of towers and tombs of many great pyramids, distinguished in their workmanship.

84.1. In the archonship of Charondas at Athens, the consular office was held by Lucius Aemilius and Gaius Plotius. In their time Philip the king, having brought most of the Greeks into friendship, was ambitious also, having struck the Athenians with terror, to hold the leadership of Greece undisputed.

84.2. Wherefore, suddenly seizing the city of Elateia and gathering his forces into it, he resolved to make war upon the Athenians. As they were unprepared because of the peace concluded, he hoped easily to win the victory; which also was accomplished. For Elateia having been seized, some came by night reporting the capture of the city and that Philip would speedily come with his force into Attica.

84.3. The generals of the Athenians, dismayed at the strangeness of the affair, sent for the trumpeters and ordered them to sound the alarm through the whole night. The report being spread to every house, the city was on edge through fear, and the whole people, at daybreak, ran together to the theatre before the magistrates summoned them, as was the custom.

84.4. When the generals came and brought forward the informant, and he had spoken, silence and fear held the theatre, and of those accustomed to address the people none dared to give counsel; and though the herald repeatedly called for those who would speak about the common safety, no one came forward as counsellor.

84.5. There being, then, great perplexity and consternation, the multitude looked toward Demosthenes. He, coming down and urging the people to take courage, declared that they ought straightway to send envoys to Thebes and urge the Boeotians to set up jointly the struggle for freedom; for the occasion did not permit sending embassies to the other allies about an alliance. For within two days the king was expected to come into Attica, and as the march was through Boeotia, the alliance of the Boeotians alone was left, it being clear that Philip, being a friend and ally of the Boeotians, would try, on his way, to take them along into the war against the Athenians.

85.1. The people approving the speech, and the decree about the embassy having been written by Demosthenes, the people sought the most capable to speak; and Demosthenes readily responded to the need. At last, swiftly going as envoy and persuading them, he returned to Athens. The people, having doubled their existing force by the alliance of the Boeotians, took courage in their hopes.

85.2. Straightway too they appointed as generals Chares and Lysicles, and sent the soldiers in full force, with their arms, into Boeotia. All the young men eagerly going to the struggle, these, marching in haste, came to Chaeronea in Boeotia; and the Boeotians, marvelling at the swiftness of the Athenians' coming, and themselves falling short in no zeal, came out with their arms, and encamping jointly, awaited the enemy's approach.

85.3. Philip at first sent envoys to the council of the Boeotians, of whom the most notable was Python. For he, famed for his power of speech, and compared among the Boeotians with Demosthenes in the speech about the alliance, surpassed all the others, but appeared inferior to him.

85.4. And Demosthenes himself, as having accomplished some great thing, in the speeches written by him takes pride in his oration against this orator, in which he says: "Then I did not give way to Python, who was bold and flowing in full stream against you."

85.5. After this Philip, having failed of the alliance of the Boeotians, nonetheless resolved to contend against both; wherefore, having waited for the laggard allies, he came into Boeotia, having foot more than thirty thousand and horse no fewer than two thousand.
85.6. Both sides being ready for the battle, in spirit and eagerness, and moreover in valour they were evenly matched, but in numbers and in excellence of generalship the king had the advantage.

85.7. For having contended in many and varied pitched battles and having been victorious in most of his battles, he had great experience in the works of war. But among the Athenians the best of their generals had died, Iphicrates and Chabrias, and also Timotheus, and of those remaining, Chares, though the foremost, differed in no way from ordinary private men in his energy and counsel in generalship.

86.1. At daybreak, the forces being drawn up, the king stationed his son Alexander, who was but a boy in age, but conspicuous for his courage and the swiftness of his energy, on one of the wings, placing beside him the most notable of the commanders; and he himself, having the picked men with him, held the command of the other part, and arranged the several divisions fittingly to the present occasion.

86.2. The Athenians, making the division of their array by nations, handed over one part to the Boeotians, and themselves held the command of the rest. A fierce battle taking place for a long time, and many falling on both sides, for a while the struggle held the hopes of victory in doubt.

86.3. After this, as Alexander was ambitious to display his own valour to his father, and left no excess of ambition behind, and likewise many brave men fought beside him, he was first to break the unbroken line of the enemy's array, and striking down many, wore down those drawn up against him.

86.4. The same being done also by those who stood beside him, the unbroken line of the array was ever being broken through. And many corpses being heaped up, Alexander's men, first forcing those drawn up against them, routed them. After this the king himself too, risking himself in the forefront and not yielding even to Alexander the credit of the victory, first thrust out by force those ranged against him, and then, compelling them to flee, became the author of the victory.
86.5. Of the Athenians there fell in the battle more than a thousand, and there were taken no fewer than two thousand.

86.6. Likewise too of the Boeotians many were slain, and not a few taken alive. After the battle Philip, setting up a trophy and granting the dead for burial, sacrificed victory-offerings to the gods and honoured according to their worth those who had distinguished themselves.

87.1. Some say that, having drunk much unmixed wine during the drinking, and holding with his friends a victory-revel, he walked through the midst of the captives, outraging with words the misfortunes of the unlucky. Demades the orator, who at that time was among the captives, used freedom of speech and uttered a saying able to check the king's wantonness.

87.2. For they say he said: "O King, when fortune has cast about you the role of Agamemnon, are you not ashamed to do the deeds of Thersites?" And Philip, moved by the aptness of the rebuke, so changed his whole disposition that he cast away his crowns, and put off the symbols of his wantonness that accompanied the revel, and admired the man who had used freedom of speech, and releasing him from captivity, took him to himself with honour.

87.3. And at last, charmed by Demades with Attic graces, he released all the captives without ransom, and, wholly laying aside the arrogance that came from the victory, sent envoys to the people of the Athenians and made with them friendship and alliance, but, putting a garrison into Thebes, granted peace to the Boeotians.

88.1. The Athenians, after the defeat, condemned to death the general Lysicles, on the accusation of Lycurgus the orator. For he, having the greatest dignity of the orators of that time, and having administered the revenues of the city for twelve years in praiseworthy fashion, and having lived a life celebrated for virtue, was a most bitter accuser in his speeches.

88.2. One may know the worth and bitterness of his speeches in the words in which, accusing Lysicles, he says: "You were general, O Lysicles, and when a thousand citizens had died, and two thousand had become captives, and a trophy stood over the city, and all Greece was enslaved, and all these things having come to pass while you led and commanded, you dare to live and to behold the light of the sun and to thrust yourself into the market-place, having become a memorial of shame and reproach to your native land."

88.3. A peculiar thing happened to occur in the period under consideration. For at the very time when the battle about Chaeronea took place, another pitched battle was joined in Italy, on the same day and hour, the Tarentines warring against the Lucanians, and Archidamus the king of the Lacedaemonians fighting alongside the Tarentines, when it happened that Archidamus himself too was slain.
88.4. He, then, ruled the Lacedaemonians twenty-three years, and his son Agis, succeeding to the kingship, ruled nine years.
88.5. While these things were going on, Timotheus the tyrant of Heracleia in Pontus died after ruling fifteen years, and his brother Dionysius, succeeding to the tyranny, ruled thirty-two years.

89.1. In the archonship of Phrynichus at Athens, the Romans appointed as consuls Titus Manlius Torquatus and Publius Decius. In their time Philip the king, elated by the victory at Chaeronea and having struck with terror the most notable cities, was ambitious to become leader of all Greece.

89.2. Spreading abroad a report that he wished to take up war against the Persians on behalf of the Greeks and to exact from them justice for the lawlessness committed against the temples, he made the Greeks his own in their goodwill. Behaving graciously toward all, both privately and publicly to the cities, he declared that he wished to confer about matters of common advantage.

89.3. Wherefore, a common council being gathered at Corinth, conferring about the war against the Persians and holding out great hopes, he urged the councillors to war. At last the Greeks, having chosen him general with full powers of Greece, he made great preparations for the campaign against the Persians. Having assigned to each city the number of soldiers for the alliance, he returned to Macedonia. And the affairs of Philip were in this state.

90.1. In Sicily Timoleon the Corinthian, having set right all things for the Syracusans and the Sicilian Greeks, died, having been general eight years. The Syracusans, having greatly esteemed the man both for his virtue and the magnitude of his benefactions, buried him magnificently, and at his funeral, the multitude being gathered, Demetrius, who was the loudest-voiced of the heralds of that time, proclaimed this decree: "The people of the Syracusans has voted to bury this Timoleon the son of Timaenetus the Corinthian at a cost of two hundred minae, and to honour him for all time with musical and equestrian and gymnastic contests, because, having overthrown the tyrants and subdued the barbarians and resettled the greatest of the Greek cities, he became the author of freedom for the Sicilian Greeks."

90.2. About the same time Ariobarzanes died after reigning twenty-six years, and Mithridates, succeeding to the kingdom, ruled thirty-five years. The Romans, arrayed against the Latins and Campanians about the city of Suessa, were victorious and took away part of the land of the defeated. And Manlius the consul, who had won the battle, celebrated a triumph.

91.1. In the archonship of Pythodorus at Athens, the Romans appointed as consuls Quintus Publius and Tiberius Aemilius Mamercus, and the hundred and eleventh Olympiad was held, in which Cleomantis of Cleitor won the foot-race.

91.2. In their time Philip the king, having been appointed leader by the Greeks and having begun the war against the Persians, sent Attalus and Parmenion ahead into Asia, giving them a part of his force and ordering them to free the Greek cities, while he himself, being eager to undertake the war with the consent of the gods, asked the Pythia whether he would conquer the king of the Persians. She gave him this oracle: "The bull is wreathed, the end is at hand, there is one who will sacrifice."

91.3. Philip, then, the oracle being ambiguous, interpreted the saying to his own advantage, as if the oracle were foretelling that the Persian would be sacrificed in the manner of a victim; but the truth was not so, but on the contrary it signified that, in a festal assembly and at the sacrifices of the gods, Philip, like the bull, wreathed, would be slaughtered.

91.4. Nevertheless, thinking that the gods were allied with him, he was exceedingly glad, as if Asia were to be a captive under the Macedonians. Straightway, then, he performed magnificent sacrifices to the gods and celebrated the marriage of his daughter Cleopatra, by Olympias, marrying her to Alexander the king of the Epirotes, who was the full brother of Olympias.

91.5. And, together with the honours to the gods, wishing as many of the Greeks as possible to share in the feasting, he held magnificent musical contests and brilliant banquets for his friends and guests.

91.6. Wherefore, from all Greece he summoned his personal guest-friends, and ordered his own friends to bring along as many as possible of their acquaintances from abroad. For he was very ambitious to behave graciously toward the Greeks and, in return for the honours of the whole leadership given him, to repay them with the appropriate intercourse.

92.1. At last, many flocking together from all sides to the festival, and the contests and the marriage being celebrated in Aegae of Macedonia, not only individually did the notable men crown him with golden crowns, but also most of the considerable cities, among which was that of the Athenians too.

92.2. As this crown was being proclaimed by the herald, it said at the end that, if anyone, having plotted against King Philip, should flee to the Athenians, he should be given up. By the self-prompted utterance, as by some divine providence, the divine power signified the plot that was to come straightway against Philip.

92.3. In keeping with these, certain other voices too, as if inspired, occurred, foreshowing the catastrophe of the king. For at the royal drinking-party Neoptolemus the tragic actor, foremost in loudness of voice and in repute, when Philip ordered him to recite some of his successful poems and especially those pertaining to the campaign against the Persians, the artist, judging that the poem would be taken as fitting to Philip's crossing, and wishing to rebuke the prosperity of the Persian king, great and celebrated though it was, in order that it might one day, by fortune, change to its opposite, began to speak this poem: "Your thoughts now reach higher than the upper air,
and the cornfields of great plains,
your thoughts overpass house upon house,
in your folly marking out your life
to stretch far ahead.
But one comes, treading the swift-footed dark path,
and suddenly, unseen, draws near,
taking away the long hopes
of mortals: many-toiling Hades."
And he strung together the lines that follow these, all tending to the same thought.

92.4. Philip, pleased at what was recited, was wholly and utterly carried away in his mind toward the catastrophe of the Persian king, and at the same time reckoned up the Pythian oracle, having a thought similar to those spoken by the tragic actor.

92.5. At last the drinking-party broke up, and the contests beginning on the next day, the multitude, while it was still night, ran together to the theatre, and at daybreak, the procession taking place, along with the other magnificent furnishings, images of the twelve gods were carried in procession, wrought with extraordinary craftsmanship and marvellously adorned with the brilliance of wealth; and along with these a thirteenth, god-fitting image of Philip himself was carried in procession, the king displaying himself enthroned together with the twelve gods.

93.1. The theatre being filled, Philip himself came, wearing a white cloak, and having ordered the bodyguards, standing far off from him, to follow; for he showed to all that, being guarded by the common goodwill of the Greeks, he had no need of the guard of bodyguards.
93.2. Such being the height of his pre-eminence, and all praising and at the same time felicitating the man, a surprising and wholly unexpected plot and death against the king appeared.

93.3. But that the account of these things may be clear, we shall set forth beforehand the causes of the plot. Pausanias was by birth a Macedonian, from the region called Orestis, and a bodyguard of the king, and through his beauty had become a friend of Philip.

93.4. This man, seeing that another Pausanias, of the same name as himself, was beloved by the king, used reproachful words to him, saying that he was a hermaphrodite and readily received the loves of any who wished.

93.5. He, not bearing the insult from the abuse, kept silent for the present, but having communicated with a certain Attalus, one of his friends, about what he intended to do, voluntarily and surprisingly removed himself from life.

93.6. For a few days later, Philip contending against Pleurias the king of the Illyrians, Pausanias, standing before the king, received in his own body all the blows that were borne against him, and died.

93.7. The deed being noised abroad, Attalus, who was one of those of the court and very powerful with the king, invited Pausanias to dinner, and filling him with much unmixed wine, handed over his body to the muleteers for outrage and drunken wantonness such as a harlot suffers.

93.8. He, sobering from his drunkenness and being grievously pained at the outrage to his body, accused Attalus before the king. Philip was provoked at the lawlessness of the deed, but because of his connection with Attalus and his usefulness for the present, did not wish to take action against him.

93.9. For Attalus was a nephew of Cleopatra, the woman the king had married, and had been appointed general over the force sent ahead into Asia, and was brave in the struggles of war. Wherefore the king, wishing to soften the just anger of Pausanias arising from his suffering, bestowed on him considerable gifts and advanced him with honour in the bodyguard.

94.1. But Pausanias, keeping his anger unalterable, was eager to take vengeance not only from the perpetrator, but also from the one who did not avenge him. Most of all the sophist Hermocrates contributed to this resolve. For Pausanias, being his pupil, and during the lecture asking how one might become most famous, the sophist answered: "If he should slay the one who has done the greatest deeds; for, by the memory of him, the one who made away with him would be included as well."

94.2. Referring the saying to his own anger, and, through his passion, making no postponement of the resolution, he set up the plot in the very contests then taking place, in some such manner as this.

94.3. Stationing horses at the gates, he came to the entrances of the theatre, having a Celtic dagger concealed. When Philip ordered the friends who attended him to go on ahead into the theatre, and the bodyguards were standing apart, seeing the king alone, he ran up, and dealing a thrust through the ribs, stretched out the king a corpse, and himself ran toward the gates and the horses prepared for the flight.

94.4. Straightway some of the bodyguards rushed to the body of the king, while others poured out in pursuit of the murderer, among whom were Leonnatus and Perdiccas and Attalus. Pausanias, having got a lead of the pursuit, would have outstripped it by leaping onto his horse, had not his sandal caught about a certain vine and he fell. Wherefore Perdiccas and his men, overtaking him as he was rising from the ground, ran him through and slew him.

95.1. Philip, then, having become the greatest of the kings in Europe in his time, and through the magnitude of his rule having counted himself enthroned together with the twelve gods, met with such an end of his life, having ruled twenty-four years.

95.2. This king is held to have taken over the slenderest resources for the monarchy, but to have acquired the greatest of the monarchies among the Greeks, and to have increased his leadership not so much through valour in arms as through intercourse and graciousness in words.
95.3. And they say that Philip himself prided himself more on his shrewdness in generalship and on his successes through intercourse than on his courage in battles;
95.4. for of the successes in the struggles all who campaigned shared, but of the successes that came through intercourse he alone received the credit.

95.5. But we, since we have arrived at the death of Philip, shall here close this book, according to the purpose set forth at the beginning, and shall make the next the starting-point of the following.
